summary: High‑level technical deep dive covering practical artifact delivery for air‑gapped installs, offline license enforcement, GPU driver compatibility, and runtime tuning (KV cache, batching, quantization tradeoffs). topics: runtime performance: KV cache, batching, quantization
air‑gapped control plane options and KMS
transcript:
[00:00:00] Aisha: Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. We're here to walk through the on‑prem install runbook and the offline license flow for Project Nighthawk. Quick check — audio good?
[00:00:08] Ellen: Yep, loud and clear.
[00:00:10] Rafael: good here.
[00:00:12] Marcus: Awesome. I'll start with a quick overview of how we package artifacts for air‑gapped installs, and then dive into runtime expectations and driver constraints.
[00:00:22] Tom: We mainly care about the artifact handoff protocol — making sure hashes, signatures, and an automated verify step exist, rather than manual copy.
[00:00:29] Marcus: Exactly. Our typical approach is: we produce a signed tarball per component (serving runtime, model bundle, operator images), attach a SHA256 manifest, and a GPG signature. For air‑gap, we provide an encrypted USB option plus an SFTP drop in exceptional cases.
[00:00:44] Mina: When you say signed tarball, what keys do you use? We need to know how this chains to our KMS/HSM for verification.
[00:00:51] Aisha: We'll provide a Redwood release signing key public fingerprint and a short verification script. For long‑term we can support customer‑provided GPG keys if you want to re‑sign after verification.
[00:01:00] Rafael: Are those manifests deterministic? We want to ensure the model bundle hash doesn't change with metadata.
[00:01:05] Marcus: We canonicalize tar creation: sorted entries, fixed timestamps, and strip extended attrs. That makes the SHA256 stable. Occasionally the OS tar differs, so we ship our verify container that computes and validates the manifest.
[00:01:20] Tom: Good. On drivers — our infra team is strict about CUDA and driver versions. What exactly do you require?
[00:01:26] Marcus: We support NVIDIA drivers 525.x and up for our current runtime. Preferred is 535 with CUDA 12.1 for best kernel performance. We also recommend installing DCGM for visibility. MIG is supported but we advise a specific container runtime config; we'll share an example.
[00:01:43] Rafael: 535, got it. We're on RHEL 8.6 with 5.14 kernel for most nodes. Any kernel module caveats?
[00:01:50] Marcus: Kernel modules need to match the driver. We'll put together a matrix: driver version vs kernel min. RHEL 8.6 is fine but note the driver installer will compile the nvidia modules unless you use the distro packages. If you air‑gap, include the kernel headers in the artifact.
[00:02:03] Mina: For security, we need signed drivers. We have driver module signature enforcement enabled in our fleet. Do you support signing the kernel modules?
[00:02:10] Marcus: We can provide signed modules or a deployable kmod-signing keypair. Two options: Redwood signs modules with our vendor key (we provide public cert), or you supply a customer MOK and we sign during onsite install. Both are doable but we need advance notice.
[00:02:25] Ellen: What's the offline license enforcement model? We can't have phones home.
[00:02:29] Aisha: For air‑gapped customers we provide a time‑boxed license file tied to host identifiers (NIC MACs or K8s node UUIDs). The license is signed and validated locally by a license daemon. No external checks by default.
[00:02:41] Tom: Host identifiers are flaky — we prefer a hardware TPM endorsement key. Can the license be bound to TPM EK or PCRs?
[00:02:47] Marcus: Yes, we support TPM binding as an option. The license payload can include a TPM public ephemeral assertion. We also support a cluster‑level license keyed by a customer‑generated HSM attest token provided during the install window.
[00:02:58] Mina: How do you handle clock skew? If license is time‑boxed, networkless machines may have bad clocks.
[00:03:03] Marcus: We recommend including a grace leeway (e.g., 48 hours) and requiring a manual renewal token for extensions. The license daemon uses either hardware RTC or the K8s control plane time; we'll add guidance to the runbook for NTP best practices in isolated environments.
[00:03:16] Rafael: On the model bundles — do you ship quantized variants? We want to test int8 vs fp16 for throughput.
[00:03:23] Marcus: We can provide multiple variants. For Nighthawk we recommend two sets: a fp16 baseline and an int8 quantized candidate using our quantization pipeline. The artifact will include both weights and a small validation prompt set so you can run accuracy regression locally.
[00:03:36] Tom: Nice — will the runtime auto‑select quantized model or is that a config toggle?
[00:03:40] Marcus: It's a config toggle per serving route. You can do A/B rollouts in the same cluster with a canary percentage. For air‑gap, the console that administers rollouts can be local, but the APIs are identical.
[00:03:50] Ellen: Can you explain KV cache behavior for long‑running conversations? We have tight memory constraints per GPU.
[00:03:56] Marcus: Sure. Our runtime stores KV cache in GPU memory by default for lowest latency. We support sharded KV across multiple GPUs and an optional pinned CPU fallback when GPU memory is constrained. Cache eviction strategies are LRU with tunable TTLs. We'll ship a recommended starting profile for sequence length distributions you provided.
[00:04:13] Rafael: How about batching? We want throughput, but tail latency matters for our interactive customers.
[00:04:17] Marcus: Continuous batching with size/cutoff policies. You set a max batch and a latency SLO. For interactive, we suggest small max batch (4–8) and a short latency cutoff (30–40ms) to avoid head‑of‑line. For high throughput async workloads, increase batch to 32–64. There's also dynamic batching where we inform the kernel about typical sequence length to optimize memory planning.
[00:04:36] Mina: Any concerns with quantization interacting with KV cache fidelity? We get hallucinations when precision drops.
[00:04:41] Marcus: Good point. int8 can change activation distributions slightly; for chat you might want fp16 for the final token scoring. We support hybrid paths: compute attention in int8 but maintain some high‑precision internal accumulators. The evaluation bundle helps you check exact regression numbers.
[00:04:58] Aisha: I'm going to pause on the technical bits to cover the artifact delivery logistics. We do three packages: core runtime, model bundles, and ops tooling (helm charts and CRs). Each package has a signed manifest and an install script. For air‑gap, we can deliver a sealed USB plus an encrypted archive; for on‑prem with restricted egress, we can ship a jump host tar that you rsync from.
[00:05:20] Rafael: Will you encrypt the USB with our public key? We prefer we generate the keypair and you encrypt to our pubkey.
[00:05:25] Aisha: Yes, we can encrypt to your provided PGP key. That means you need to share the public key in advance. We also sign the archive with our private key so you can verify origin.
[00:05:33] Jordan: And the verify script will perform: signature verification, SHA256 manifest check, sample model load sanity run, and GPU driver check. It emits a machine‑parsable json report.
[00:05:44] Tom: Great. For the driver matrix, we need examples for both containerd and docker runtime.
[00:05:49] Marcus: We'll provide both. For containerd we recommend NVIDIA container toolkit, and for Docker we list the docker‑nvidia shim specifics. We'll include a shim configuration that handles GPU isolation and adjusts cgroup settings for low latency.
[00:06:02] Mina: About control plane — do you require the Redwood control plane for telemetry?
[00:06:07] Aisha: No. In Private mode you can run with a completely private control plane. There are two options: 1) full local control plane that hosts the console and telemetry store on your network, or 2) hybrid where telemetry is queued locally and forwarded through a customer‑managed egress jump host. For air‑gapped with strict policy, we do local only.
[00:06:24] Mina: If we do local only, how do you handle alerting and support?
[00:06:28] Aisha: We provide a support bundle script that collects logs and produces an encrypted bundle you can share via SFTP or USB to our support team. For urgent issues we offer a signed on‑site engineer visit under the SOW.
[00:06:38] Ellen: On SLA — are latency SLAs impacted by air‑gap? Also do you still support live model rollouts?
[00:06:44] Marcus: The runtime's latency properties are identical. The difference is rollout speed — without internet our deployment manager operates locally so rollouts are as fast as your network and operator cadence. SLAs stay the same but note that remote fallbacks (e.g., auto‑fallback to hosted variants) are disabled in fully air‑gapped installs.
[00:06:58] Rafael: Is there an option to allow limited egress for telemetry only?
[00:07:02] Aisha: Yes, we can configure a one‑way egress tunnel that only sends aggregated telemetry (no payloads). That requires your security approval and can be throttled.
[00:07:11] Tom: Back to GPU drivers — you mentioned DCGM. Does Redwood depend on DCGM for autoscaling or only for metrics?
[00:07:17] Marcus: Only for metrics and health checks. We don't require DCGM for correctness. If DCGM isn't available we fall back to node exporter metrics, but ops visibility is reduced.
[00:07:25] Mina: For driver lifecycle, we want a non‑disruptive upgrade path. Can you do rolling driver updates without reboots?
[00:07:31] Marcus: If you use vendor packaged drivers that support module livepatching you can avoid reboots, but generally kernel module replacement requires either reboot or driver unload which is disruptive. We can coordinate a maintenance window and ship precompiled modules for your kernel to reduce downtime.
[00:07:46] Rafael: Will you provide prebuilt RPMs/debs for offline install?
[00:07:49] Marcus: Yes, we can provide distro‑specific packages and also the driver installer tarball. For RHEL we will provide an RPM bundle including kernel headers.
[00:07:57] Ellen: What about licensing for additional nodes mid‑contract? Is there a fast offline path?
[00:08:02] Aisha: We have a token‑based offline license extension. You request a one‑time extension token by sending a signed CSR containing the new node IDs; we generate a signed token that you can load locally. The manual flow takes <24 hours typically.
[00:08:15] Tom: Great. For runtime perf: can you share expected QPS per GPU for our model size? We sent you logs from an FP16 baseline earlier.
[00:08:22] Marcus: Based on your 13B model baseline, expectation is ~65–80 tokens/s per GPU for single‑stream low latency, and up to 300–400 tokens/s when batching (batch 32). These are ballpark and depend on sequence length. We'll include tuned kernel flags we used to benchmark.
[00:08:39] Rafael: Are those numbers with KV cache on GPU?
[00:08:41] Marcus: Yes, GPU KV on for those numbers. With CPU fallback KV you lose ~20–30% throughput but can support higher concurrency.
[00:08:50] Mina: Any guidance on memory reservation for the OS vs runtime to avoid OOMs?
[00:08:54] Marcus: Reserve 10% for host processes, and ensure GPU reserved memory for CUDA context with --gpu‑mem‑reserve at container startup. We'll include a sample manifest that sets node allocatable and kubelet flags.
[00:09:07] Jordan: I'm dropping a link in the chat — it's the provisional install runbook URL (internal) and a short artifact checklist.
[00:09:11] [link omitted in transcript]
[00:09:13] Ellen: I have one compliance question — do you produce audit logs for license operations and model loads? We need an immutable trail.
[00:09:19] Marcus: Yes — the local control plane writes signed audit events to an append‑only log. We support shipping the audit log to a remote syslog collector if you have one. The log format is JSON‑L with signatures.
[00:09:31] Mina: Are those logs encrypted at rest by default?
[00:09:34] Marcus: Yes, we encrypt at rest using your KMS or our default local encryption. For air‑gapped, you'll likely supply the KMS wrapping key or we can store the wrapping key on a hardware security module.
[00:09:44] Rafael: What's the expected size of the artifact USB? Our operations team is strict about incidentally high capacities.
[00:09:49] Aisha: Typical sealed USB is 64–128GB depending on model variants. If you only want a minimal installer it's under 8GB. We can also provide split archives.
[00:09:57] Tom: For the sample verify script, can you make it exit non‑zero on any mismatch so our CI can gate the install?
[00:10:02] Jordan: Yes, verify script returns machine JSON and non‑zero code on failure. We'll provide a small wrapper that integrates with Ansible or other configuration management.
[00:10:11] Rafael: One more — if we decide to run the console locally, what are the DB requirements?
[00:10:15] Marcus: Minimal production install uses Postgres 13 and an object store (S3 compatible). For air‑gapped you can use MinIO. We document recommended sizing based on retention (we default 30 days). If you want longer retention, we recommend sharding and a larger DB.
[00:10:29] Ellen: OK, sounds good. Let's recap next steps.
[00:10:31] Aisha: Recap: Redwood to deliver signed artifacts + public GPG fingerprint; Marcus to provide driver compatibility matrix and quantized model bundles; Nighthawk to confirm node counts and provide public PGP key; arrange onsite window week of 7/21. Anything else?
[00:10:44] Mina: Please add the module signing options in writing — we need that for procurement.
[00:10:48] Aisha: Will do.
[00:10:50] Tom: We'll follow up with a short spreadsheet of node details after this call.
[00:10:54] Rafael: Expect that by EOD tomorrow.
[00:10:57] Aisha: Perfect. Thanks everyone. We'll send the artifact checklist and the verify script in the next two business days.
[00:11:04] Ellen: Thank you.
[00:11:06] [end of recorded transcript — remainder of meeting was a brief Q&A and off‑line scheduling which is summarized in action items]
